newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israel says Arab peace demands old hat.
newsitem.headline: Israel says Arab peace demands old hat.

text.p: Israel said on Thursday that Arab conditions for peace talks were a hangover from the past now that they were talking with the Jewish state.
Foreign Minister David Levy told a news conference in Cairo that the talks were the way to overcome the obstacles stalling the peace process and talk of conditions would not help.
"The peace process is truly a road that has no alternative," Levy said after talks with Egyptian counterpart Amr Moussa.

"It is in discussing that one resolves problems... We are already holding talks. We have recognised one another, the principles and also the need to talk -- that's why I say that those conditions are of the past," he added.
He was answering a question on whether Israel still recognised the principle of land for peace -- in Arab eyes the basis of the peace talks launched in Madrid in 1991.

Levy's comments will confirm Arab anxieties about the intentions of the rightwing government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has both promised to fulfil old agreements and questioned the land-for-peace concept.
Egypt told Israel on Thursday that it could not impose a balanced peace on the Palestinians and insisted that the talks should follow the Madrid framework.

"Peace, in order to last...has to be balanced between the Israelis and the Palestinians, not to be imposed but to be agreed upon," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told reporters after Levy met Egypt's Hosni Mubarak.
"We look forward to the acceleration of the pace of the talks along the lines accepted by us all," he added.

Peace negotiations with Syria are stalled over Netanyahu's refusal to hand over the Golan Heights Israel occupied in a 1967 war. Talks on the Lebanese track are also frozen over withdrawal from a southern buffer zone.

Negotiations with the Palestinians are currently snagged on a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron as stipulated by a peace agreement which Netanayahu is trying to alter for security reasons.
The Palestinians say the deal should be implemented as is, a demand Israel says is slowing the whole process down.
"The issue of Hebron in the eyes of the Palestinians is not an issue on its own," key Israeli negotiator Dan Shomron told Israel Radio on Thursday.

"They see the entire process and want, via the conclusion of the protocol on Hebron, to also put in issues that are connected to the entire process and this causes great difficulty in concluding," he added.
But Moussa, whose country became in 1979 the first Arab state to make peace with Israel, said he thought it was Israel, and not Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, that was stalling.
"It takes two (to slow down the peace process) anyway and it was not Mr. Arafat," he said.

Netanyahu's policies, which included lifting a ban on building Jewish settlements on Palestinian lands, have sparked international condemnation and jeopardised the Jewish state's ties with Arab allies like Jordan.
Even Shomron, a former Israeli army chief of staff, said he thought Palestinian concerns about the continuation of the peace process were valid.
"They have...are real concerns... regarding the continuation of the peace process, the redeployment not only in Hebron, continuation of the redeployment," he said, but did not elaborate further.
Mubarak has said he would not meet Netanyahu unless both sides reached an agreement on Hebron, home of 400 Jewish settlers whose security Netanyahu is trying to ensure.
Palestinians view the settlers as a provocation and Arafat has demanded Netanyahu curb a minister who has said settlement of occupied lands will dramatically increase.
In Washington, a senior U.S. official said on Thursday that Israel risked losing its prosperity unless it pursued the peace process with its neighbours.

Under Secretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat also charged that Israel was imposing a host of bureaucratic regulations that were "choking the economy" of Palestinian self-rule territories under the guise of protecting Israeli security.

Eizenstat told the Washington Institute, a Middle East think tank, it was "important for Israelis to understand" that the peace process had raised their standard of living, boosting foreign investment and keeping unemployment low.
"Israel is in effect open to the world, and the world is increasingly open to Israeli products, and it is the peace process which has created the enabling environment to make this possible," he said.
